areas.name: Cathays Park
areas.reason: The Edwardian civic centre, Cardiff Castle, Bute Park and the Victorian villas of Park Place and North Road, all standing in 1947, form a grouping of exceptional architectural and historic interest.

reasons: Castle's Roman-to-Burges fabric and Blackfriars remains record the town's origins (City Centre appraisal pp.10, 110).
Rise to civic and capital status; the 1897 Bute land sale shaped the plan (City Centre appraisal p.110).
Portland-stone civic ensemble Newman called the 'finest Civic Centre in the British Isles' (City Centre appraisal p.10).
National War Memorial, Gorsedd Gardens and City Hall lawn: national commemoration (City Centre appraisal pp.10, 18).

areas.name: Charles Street
areas.reason: One of Cardiff's earliest planned streets (1850s): stuccoed Italianate terraces, two landmark churches and, in 1947, a complete southern end to Bridge Street with the Wesleyan Central Hall.

reasons: 1850s plots, setted rear lanes and stucco fronts of pre-1870s growth (City Centre appraisal pp.34, 37, 39).
Residential street turned business street as Queen Street grew from the 1870s (City Centre appraisal p.34).
Uniform stucco town houses; a rare glimpse of pre-expansion Cardiff (City Centre appraisal p.34).
St David's Cathedral, Ebenezer, Friends Meeting House and the 1947 Central Hall (City Centre appraisal p.35; HER 01136s).

areas.name: Churchill Way (Pembroke Terrace and Edward Terrace)
areas.reason: In 1947 the area was two facing Victorian terraces, Pembroke Terrace and Edward Terrace, on either bank of the open tree-lined East Bute Dock Feeder.

reasons: Paired-villa plots and the line of the culverted dock feeder (City Centre appraisal pp.48, 109).
Villas beside Bute's open dock feeder, offices from 1888; culverting began 1947 (City Centre appraisal pp.48-52).
Waterside Gothic villas framing the tree-lined feeder, closed by Harris's 1877 chapel (City Centre appraisal pp.48, 51).
Welsh Calvinistic Methodist chapel and Pembroke Terrace war memorial (HER 01139s, 05881s).

areas.name: Queen Street
areas.reason: Cardiff's principal commercial street of 1880-1939, extended in 1947 to its eastern end at Station Terrace, where the Capitol Cinema, Cory Hall and the Taff Vale Railway offices stood.

reasons: Burgage plot widths record medieval Crockherbtown (City Centre appraisal pp.63, 108).
Shopping's shift from St Mary Street; coal-era wealth 1880s-1930s (City Centre appraisal pp.71, 110).
Individual stone frontages, Gothic Revival to Art Deco, on a curving street (City Centre appraisal pp.64, 71).
Capitol, Empire, Olympia, Park Hall and Cory Hall: the city's leisure and meeting centre (graded A4-12, A5-18, A5-20).

areas.name: Windsor Place
areas.reason: Mid-19th-century planned merchant suburb of Windsor Place, St Andrew's Crescent and Park Place. In 1947 it was unbroken by Stuttgarter Strasse and continued east into Dumfries Place.

reasons: c.1860 lime avenue and St Andrew's Crescent oval survive from the layout (City Centre appraisal p.95).
Early suburb under Bute and Tredegar leasing; professional offices after 1889 (City Centre appraisal pp.85, 110).
Best preserved mid-19th-century houses in the centre; Burges's Park House (City Centre appraisal pp.89-90).
Dewi Sant, City URC and Windsor Place Congregational chapel (City Centre appraisal p.89; HER 05871s).

areas.name: St Mary Street, The Hayes and the Canal Wharves
areas.reason: The medieval street pattern and late-Victorian commercial core with its arcades and market, which in 1947 still ran east across The Hayes and south along the working Glamorganshire Canal wharves.

reasons: Burgage plots, Womanby Street warehouses and the 1947 canal wharves (St Mary Street appraisal pp.5-6, 18).
Civic and commercial centre before Cathays Park; canal carrying Merthyr iron (St Mary Street appraisal pp.6-7).
Continuous Victorian and Edwardian frontages and arcades (City Centre appraisal p.111).
Market, arcades, Hayes open-air market and civic celebrations (St Mary Street appraisal p.7).

areas.name: Tredegarville
areas.reason: The Tredegar estate's 1850s suburb of four streets: The Parade, The Walk, West Grove and East Grove. In 1947 it still ran south to Newport Road.

reasons: Original Pennant paving, crossing bands and Victorian street signs (Tredegarville appraisal pp.7, 12).
One of Cardiff's first suburbs, laid out by Charles Morgan of the Tredegar estate (Tredegarville appraisal pp.5, 7).
Classical stucco and Gothic Pennant villas in tree-lined streets (Tredegarville appraisal pp.9-11).
Mansion House, Baptist and Unitarian churches, schools and college (Tredegarville appraisal pp.7-8).

areas.name: Mount Stuart Square and the Bute Suburb
areas.reason: The commercial heart of the coal port around the Coal Exchange, together with the 1850s Bute-estate residential grid south of James Street from which it grew, all standing in 1947.

reasons: 20 ft plots multiplied in commercial rebuilds record suburb turning exchange quarter (MSS appraisal p.11).
Coal Exchange, where the coal price was struck; Cardiff as leading coal port (MSS appraisal p.6).
Enclosed streets mixing stucco houses and commercial palazzi with maritime carving (MSS appraisal pp.10, 22-23).
Tiger Bay seafarers settled here; Bethel, Mount Stuart and St Stephen's chapels (MSS appraisal p.6; HER 08188s).

areas.name: Pierhead
areas.reason: The sea gate of the Bute Docks: the Pierhead building, dock basins and sea walls, the Mount Stuart graving docks, the whole of Bute Crescent and the dock workers' esplanades, all standing and working in 1947.

reasons: Dock and sea walls, graving docks with gates and capstans, powerhouse (Pierhead appraisal pp.10-11, 19).
Bute West Dock (1839) and the 1896 Pierhead dock offices (Pierhead appraisal p.6; Coflein 91412).
Terracotta Pierhead, stucco Bute Crescent and esplanades set against open water (Pierhead appraisal pp.11, 14).
All Souls seamen's church and Norwegian church; Wales' oldest multi-ethnic community (HER 08189s, 08725s; Coflein 420177).

areas.name: Loudoun Square and North Butetown (Tiger Bay)
areas.reason: The Bute estate's 1850s planned residential suburb around Loudoun Square and Bute Street. By 1947 it was home to Wales' oldest multi-ethnic seafaring community, whose chapels, missions, mosque and Greek church shaped its character.

reasons: 1850s grid intact in 1947; chapel and mosque sites have potential (Coflein 33120; HER 08178s, 08182s).
Bute estate's planned suburb, home of the coal port's dock labour (MSS appraisal pp.6, 30; Coflein 33120).
Formal square and Gothic chapels; modest, deteriorated fabric (Coflein 33120; Pierhead appraisal p.14).
Tiger Bay: families from about 50 countries; Wales' first purpose-built mosque, 1947 (Coflein 420177; HER 08178s).

areas.name: Newtown (the Irish quarter)
areas.reason: Six streets of small terraced houses built in 1846 for Irish dock workers, with St Paul's Roman Catholic Church and All Saints' Church on Tyndall Street. The communal interest is high but the architectural interest modest.

reasons: Unusually early planned workers' grid of 1846 (HER 05471s).
Built for Irish dock workers; famine link general knowledge, to verify (HER 05471s).
Plain two-storey terraces on narrow streets; little display beyond the churches (HER 05471s; OS six-inch 1947).
Cardiff's Irish Catholic quarter around St Paul's church, school and presbytery (Coflein 14220; HER 05468s).

areas.name: Bute Dock Heads (Atlantic Wharf and Tyndall Street)
areas.reason: The heads of the Bute West and East Docks: bonded and railway warehouses, flour mill, foundry, Junction Canal lock and the Bute graving docks with their pumping house. A dense group of 19th-century port buildings.

reasons: Dock heads, Junction Canal lock and graving docks where canal, rail and dock met (HER 01682.20s, 08050s, 08055s).
Bute East Dock (1855-59) and railway warehouses of the coal and cargo port (Coflein 91412).
Monumental Bonded Warehouse and dock engineering; a functional dockscape (graded C7-19; Coflein 34244).
Workplace of Newtown and Butetown dock workers; otherwise limited (HER 05471s).

areas.name: Glamorganshire Canal Sea Lock and Clarence Embankment
areas.reason: The canal's sea lock with its lock-keeper's house and lock hotels, the Royal Hamadryad Seamen's Hospital and the small Victorian riverside enclave of Clarence Embankment, Pomeroy Street and Harrowby Street.

reasons: Seaward end of the 1794-98 canal and the Severn defence headquarters (HER 05571s).
Canal terminus and the Royal Hamadryad seamen's hospital (HER 05063s).
Modest grid of terraces and inns beside the lock and river (OS six-inch 1947).
Seamen's hospital, Bethel chapel (congregation to 2000) and sailors' inns (HER 05918s; graded H5-10).

areas.name: Grangetown (Grange Gardens core)
areas.reason: Late-Victorian bye-law terraces around Grange Gardens, St Paul's Church and the board school. Coherent, but of standard design.

reasons: Map only: late-Victorian grid complete in 1947; 1880 presence unchecked (OS six-inch 1947).
Grid around a park on land given by Lords Bute and Windsor (Cadw PGW(Gm)72).
Standard bye-law terraces around the registered Grange Gardens (Cadw PGW(Gm)72; OS six-inch 1947).
Grange Gardens with war memorial, and St Paul's Church as neighbourhood centres (Cadw PGW(Gm)72; HER 01266s).

areas.name: Cathedral Road
areas.reason: A planned late Victorian and Edwardian Bute-estate suburb of exceptional quality, laid out on a formal grid beside Sophia Gardens and Pontcanna Fields.

reasons: Plot widths, rear lanes and coach houses record Bute estate lease control (Cathedral Road appraisal pp.12-13, 22).
3rd Marquess's estate development under Corbett, with Burges's influence (Cathedral Road appraisal p.12).
Some of the best Victorian and Edwardian architecture in Wales (Cathedral Road appraisal p.4).
Plasturton Gardens, Pontcanna Street and churches as community landmarks (Cathedral Road appraisal pp.13, 21, 23).

areas.name: Conway Road
areas.reason: The best surviving layout of the Cardiff Freehold Land Society's 1850s plots in Canton, with varied villas and terraces on a strict building line.

reasons: Plots in ten-foot multiples and building line record the Freehold Land Society sales (Conway Road appraisal p.6).
Freehold plots that gave owners the vote; probably unique in Wales (Conway Road appraisal pp.6, 8).
Tree-lined streets, landmark villas, Methodist church and corner pubs (Conway Road appraisal pp.8-10).
Methodist church, Canton Gospel Hall, pubs; former deaf and dumb school (Conway Road appraisal p.9).

areas.name: Cardiff Road
areas.reason: Generous Victorian and Edwardian villas, Howells School and a dense tree canopy on the ridge above Llandaff Fields, with the well-preserved Edwardian suburb of Palace Road and Howells Crescent.

reasons: Lias, Forest of Dean and Radyr stone record building phases from the 1850s (Cardiff Road appraisal p.13).
Merchants' villas near restored Llandaff; Howells School by Herbert Williams (Cardiff Road appraisal pp.9, 11).
Green tunnel of trees, collegiate Howells School and intact Palace Road detail (Cardiff Road appraisal pp.5, 11-13).
Howells School, the area's focus since 1860 (Cardiff Road appraisal p.11).

areas.name: Llandaff
areas.reason: A medieval cathedral city on its rock above the Taff, with the cathedral, Bishop's Palace, Bell Tower, Green, High Street and organic village streets.

reasons: Medieval street plan, palace, bell tower, Romano-British finds; cathedral from 1120 (Llandaff appraisal pp.19-20, 42-45).
Bishop's seat since the 12th century; Teilo's llan; 1941 bomb damage second only to Coventry (Llandaff appraisal pp.5, 42-43).
Fall from the Green to the cathedral, spire views and narrow streets (Llandaff appraisal pp.24-26, 32-33).
Diocesan centre and pilgrimage place; Green, Cross and war memorial (Llandaff appraisal pp.26, 43-45).

areas.name: Church Road, Whitchurch
areas.reason: Individually designed late Victorian and Edwardian houses in large gardens between Prichard's St Mary's Church and Llandaff station, built for the commuting middle class.

reasons: Pressed brick, Pennant and Radyr stone, tile-hung gables (Church Road Whitchurch appraisal pp.9-12).
Growth after the 1840s TVR station and the new St Mary's of 1885 (Church Road Whitchurch appraisal p.5).
Varied gabled houses, mature trees and high stone walls (Church Road Whitchurch appraisal pp.7-13).
Prichard's St Mary's and churchyard, the 'green heart' of the village (Church Road Whitchurch appraisal pp.8, 13).

areas.name: Melingriffith (with the tinplate works, 1947)
areas.reason: The Melingriffith tinplate works, a medieval mill site turned iron forge c.1749 and later tinplate works of Richard Thomas & Co., with its canal lock, water pump, towpath bridges, lodge, Lock Cottage, Oak Cottage and Ty Mawr. It was a complete industrial group, closed in 1942 but still standing in 1947.

reasons: Works plan, feeder, pump and canal arc; buried medieval mill and forge (Melingriffith appraisal p.8; Coflein 40456).
Senghenydd manorial mill turned Richard Thomas tinplate works; closed 1942 (Melingriffith appraisal p.6).
Riverside works group with 17th-century cottage in a wooded valley (Melingriffith appraisal pp.8, 10).
Works community in Oak Cottage, Ty Mawr, canal terrace and Lock Cottage (Melingriffith appraisal pp.6-7).

areas.name: Rhiwbina Garden Village
areas.reason: Raymond Unwin's garden village for the Housing Reform Company, begun in 1913 and run as a co-operative, in a unified Arts and Crafts 'garden village style'.

reasons: House types, original specifications, inside bathrooms and damp courses (Rhiwbina appraisal pp.6, 18).
Raymond Unwin and the Garden City Movement in Wales (Rhiwbina appraisal pp.4, 6, 8).
Unified Arts and Crafts groups that 'speak the same architectural language' (Rhiwbina appraisal p.6).
Co-operative village with houses let at cost, still so run in 1947 (Rhiwbina appraisal pp.6, 9).

areas.name: Roath Park
areas.reason: Cardiff's first publicly owned park, the Recreation Ground and Pleasure Gardens, framed by Bute-estate terraces designed under E.W.M. Corbett.

reasons: Pennant, brick, Bath stone, encaustic tiles and service lanes (Roath Park appraisal pp.12-15).
Bute's 1887 park gift tied to housing; Harpur, Pettigrew and Corbett (Roath Park appraisal p.7).
Grand terraces facing the park, 'greater than the individual parts' (Roath Park appraisal p.8).
The town's public park from 1889, with churches and a board school (Roath Park appraisal pp.7, 11).

areas.name: Roath Mill Gardens
areas.reason: Edwardian Tredegar-estate terraces around Waterloo Gardens and Roath Mill Gardens, public gardens laid out by Pettigrew, with Prichard's St Margaret's Church and Roath Court.

reasons: Brook, mill site and planned terraces (Roath Mill Gardens appraisal p.6).
Lord Tredegar's land gift; W.H. Scott houses; manorial Roath Court (Roath Mill Gardens appraisal pp.6, 8).
Unified gabled terraces enclosing the gardens; fine middle-class Edwardian housing (Roath Mill Gardens appraisal pp.6-7).
Public gardens, bowling green, tennis courts and two parish churches (Roath Mill Gardens appraisal pp.8, 12).

areas.name: Roath Park Lake and Gardens
areas.reason: Roath Park's lake, botanic gardens and wild gardens with the Scott Memorial, framed by individually designed inter-war houses and Edwardian villas on Cefn Coed Road.

reasons: Dam, bridges, glasshouse and inter-war house types (Roath Park Lake appraisal pp.10-11, 25).
Bute's 1887 gift; Scott Memorial to the Terra Nova expedition (Roath Park Lake appraisal p.8).
Long views across the lake to the hills, houses overlooking the water (Roath Park Lake appraisal pp.8, 11).
Scott Memorial a civic commemorative focus; much-used lake (Roath Park Lake appraisal pp.8, 12).

areas.name: Oakfield Street and Newport Road (1947)
areas.reason: Mid to late Victorian classical and gothic villas of the Roath Court estate on Oakfield Street, continuing along the Newport Road frontage towards Roath Court, the eastern approach to the town.

reasons: Plots follow the Roath Court estate field; classical-to-Gothic villa sequence (Oakfield Street appraisal pp.7, 10).
Williams family of Roath Court and Thomas Waring; main eastern road into town (Oakfield Street appraisal p.5).
Paired villas, tree avenue, St Anne's by J. Arthur Reeve (Oakfield Street appraisal pp.7-11).
St Anne's Church and school the local focus (Oakfield Street appraisal pp.8-9).

areas.name: Wordsworth Avenue
areas.reason: One of Cardiff's first suburbs, laid out in 1850 off Newport Road on the Tredegar estate, with Italianate stucco villas and Habershon's Woodland Place.

reasons: Stucco villas with incised rustication and a cul-de-sac plan (Wordsworth Avenue appraisal pp.6, 8-9).
'One of Cardiff's first suburbs', Tredegar estate under Charles Morgan; Habershon (Wordsworth Avenue appraisal pp.5-7).
Four-storey villas, Woodland Place courtyard group and street trees (Wordsworth Avenue appraisal pp.6-7, 9).
Mostly residential; Trevethen House school use undated (Wordsworth Avenue appraisal p.7).

areas.name: Insole Court
areas.reason: The Insole family's Victorian gothic mansion, its estate buildings and its terraced Victorian and Edwardian garden with Pulhamite rockwork.

reasons: Garden layout of 1874-1915, terraces and Pulhamite rockwork (Cadw PGW(Gm)27).
Insole coal-shipping family; Violet Insole's iris collections (Cadw PGW(Gm)27; LB 14127).
Romantic Gothic house with Burges-influenced interiors and balustraded terraces (Cadw LB 14127; PGW(Gm)27).
Corporation-owned from 1932; Cardiff ARP headquarters in WWII (Cadw LB 14127).

areas.name: Howard Gardens, Moira Terrace and Adamsdown Square
areas.reason: Adamsdown's two public squares (Howard Gardens and Adamsdown Square), Moira Terrace with its chapels, the Old Cemetery and the Board School: a planned late Victorian working- and lower-middle-class district next to Tredegarville.

reasons: Two planned squares with terraces and cemetery record Adamsdown's layout (Coflein 412164, 402727; OS six-inch 1947).
Dense Victorian suburb with Mount Tabor chapel and board school (Coflein 14217, 9348).
Terraces round small public squares; Moira Terrace the one listed group (Cadw LB 18640-18656).
Chapels, Moira Terrace synagogue use, board school and seamen's cemetery (HER 05457s; Coflein 402727).

areas.name: Riverside: Lower Cathedral Road, Despenser Gardens and Fitzhamon Embankment
areas.reason: Late Victorian Riverside terraces south of Cowbridge Road around Despenser Gardens, with the Fitzhamon Embankment frontage to the Taff and the chapels of Rawden Place and Clare Gardens.

reasons: Map only: planned terraces with back lanes and corner shops; 1880 presence unchecked (OS six-inch 1947).
Victorian westward growth facing Cathedral Road (graded B1-02, B2-09; OS six-inch 1947).
Despenser Gardens and the river frontage; plain terraces elsewhere (OS six-inch 1947).
Rawden Place, Clare Gardens and Victoria Baptist chapels (graded A1-40, C1-05, C1-24; Coflein 14279).

areas.name: Whitchurch village core (Merthyr Road and Old Church Road)
areas.reason: The old village nucleus of Whitchurch on the 1767 turnpike: early 19th-century terraces, cottages, inns and chapels between the crossroads and the new St Mary's, linked by Old Church Road to the medieval church site.

reasons: Footings of the medieval church and graveyard; turnpike street line (Coflein 307792).
Medieval chapelry of Llandaff and de Clare demesne manor; turnpike village (Church Road appraisal p.5; Coflein 307792).
Map only: building quality cannot be read on the one-inch 1947.
Tabernacle chapel, old church site and inns (Coflein 9656; Church Road appraisal p.5).

areas.name: Wyndham Crescent and Severn Road (early Canton)
areas.reason: The earliest Canton streets west of Cathedral Road: stuccoed houses on Wyndham Crescent, the first Severn Road terraces, St Catherine's (1886) and St Mary of the Angels (1907), the Severn Road school and chapels.

reasons: Stucco and early Pennant terraces from before the Bute grid (Cathedral Road appraisal p.7).
Early growth of Canton village west of Cathedral Road (Cathedral Road appraisal p.7).
Landmark churches; terraces lack open space and street trees (Cathedral Road appraisal p.7).
St Catherine's, St Mary of the Angels, chapels and the board school (Coflein 14269, 14276, 801219, 11813).

areas.name: Old St Mellons
areas.reason: Historic coaching and agricultural village on the London-Cardiff road, with medieval church, 17th-18th century inns, chapels and cottages, still detached from Cardiff in 1947.

reasons: 14th-century church, scheduled cross base, 17th-18th-century inns and 1846 tithe plots (Old St Mellons appraisal pp.4-6).
Roadside village on the London road; Ty-to-Maen gentry house (Old St Mellons appraisal pp.4-6, 27).
Organic lanes and church on its knoll above the Severn, set in fields (Old St Mellons appraisal pp.6-9).
Church, three chapels, war memorial and four pubs of a self-contained village (Old St Mellons appraisal pp.7-8).

areas.name: St Fagans
areas.reason: Outstanding estate village of the Plymouth estate around St Fagans Castle and St Mary's Church, with Michaelston-super-Ely and the wooded Ely valley as its setting.

reasons: Medieval church, Elizabethan castle on a motte site, shrunken village earthworks (St Fagans appraisal pp.4-5; Coflein 15363).
1648 Battle of St Fagans; Plymouth estate village; castle given for the museum 1947 (St Fagans appraisal pp.4-5).
Limestone and thatched cottages under the castle walls; Ely valley views (St Fagans appraisal pp.6-8, 13-14).
Estate community with church, school and inn at the castle gate (St Fagans appraisal pp.5-7).

areas.name: Pentyrch (Craig-y-Parc)
areas.reason: Rural edge of Pentyrch with farmsteads, early 20th-century houses and C.E. Mallows' Arts and Crafts house and garden at Craig-y-Parc.

reasons: Farm buildings on the 1878 map; near-complete Arts and Crafts house and garden (Craig-y-Parc appraisal pp.7, 11).
Farming hamlet becoming an early 20th-century residential group (Craig-y-Parc appraisal p.7).
Hedged fields and woods with the II* house and II* garden (Craig-y-Parc appraisal pp.9-15).
Private rural landscape; communal value modest (Craig-y-Parc appraisal pp.12, 30).

areas.name: Pentyrch (St Catwg's)
areas.reason: Old church village of Pentyrch on Church Road, with St Catwg's church, vernacular gable-end cottages, the King's Arms and Victorian houses in an enclosing valley.

reasons: Catwg's church site and well, pre-1839 vernacular group, medieval field pattern (St Catwg's appraisal pp.6, 9, 15).
Farming village; King's Arms began as the 17th-century farm Cae Golman (St Catwg's appraisal pp.6, 10).
Linear valley village focused on the church crossroads and lychgate (St Catwg's appraisal pp.9-11, 16-17).
Spout from Catwg's well was the village water supply and gossip place until the 1940s (St Catwg's appraisal pp.6-7).

areas.name: Gwaelod-y-Garth
areas.reason: Nineteenth-century ironworkers' and miners' village of stone terraces and chapels at the foot of Garth Hill above the Taff.

reasons: Stone cottages with coal holes, chapels, shafts and tramroad lines (Gwaelod-y-Garth appraisal pp.6-9).
Tied to the Pentyrch and Melingriffith works by the 1815 tramroad (Gwaelod-y-Garth appraisal p.6).
Linear green village in a wooded gorge above the Taff (Gwaelod-y-Garth appraisal pp.8-9, 14).
Salem and Bethlehem chapels, school, hall and inn of a Welsh-speaking community (Gwaelod-y-Garth appraisal pp.6, 10).

areas.name: Tongwynlais village
areas.reason: Taff-gorge industrial village of a 1767 roadside terrace, 19th-century terraces, four chapels, an 1877 church, a 17th-century farmhouse and canal-side corn mills.

reasons: Dated 1767 terrace, 17th-century farmhouse and canal-fed corn mills (Cadw 13916, 13914; Coflein 91482).
Turnpike and canal village of the Taff corridor to Merthyr (Cadw 13916; Coflein 91465).
Tight village of listed terraces below Castell Coch; townscape partly general knowledge (Cadw 24400-24408).
Four chapels, parish church and inns of a chapel-going community (Coflein 9655, 9653, 9436, 9647).

areas.name: Llanedeyrn church hamlet
areas.reason: Medieval church, 17th-century inn and glebe cottage of the rural parish of Llanedeyrn, isolated in fields in 1947.

reasons: Medieval church fabric, listed II*, and a thick-walled 17th-18th-century inn (Cadw 13868, 13869).
Pre-suburban parish centre before the post-war estates (Coflein 419447).
Church and inn paired at a rural junction (Cadw 13868, 13869; OS one-inch 1947).
Parish church and inn, the shared buildings of a scattered parish (Cadw 13868, 13869).

areas.name: Llanishen church crossroads
areas.reason: Old Llanishen at the church crossroads: 12th-century St Isan's, the 18th-century Church Inn, Llanishen Grange and Old House, with Victorian villas and chapel on Fidlas Road.

reasons: 12th-century church fabric, listed II*, beside a medieval grange site (Cadw 13726; Coflein 19182).
Village becoming a railway commuter suburb by 1922 (Coflein 418883).
Church, inn and cottages at a crossroads with 1870s-1900 villas (Cadw 13813, 14135, 25797).
Parish church, inn and Methodist chapel (Cadw 13726, 13813, 21575).

areas.name: Lisvane church group
areas.reason: Rural parish centre of Lisvane: 14th-century St Denys at the road junction with Arts and Crafts houses of 1906-1931 around it.

reasons: 14th-century church fabric, listed II* (Cadw 13867).
Parish church of a farming parish turning villa suburb (Cadw 13867, 23228).
Church at a rural junction; 1931 Arts and Crafts houses (Cadw 23228, 23232).
Parish church of a dispersed parish (Cadw 13867; Coflein 409952).

areas.name: Pentyrch village (Pen-y-garn / Heol-y-Pentre)
areas.reason: Upper Pentyrch at the Pen-y-garn crossroads, with Horeb (1838) and Bronllwyn chapels and cottage rows, north of the St Catwg's church village.

reasons: 1838 chapel and early cottage rows (Cadw 22821; OS one-inch 1947).
The parish's nonconformist focus beside the church village (St Catwg's appraisal p.6).
Map only for the cottages: small crossroads group (OS one-inch 1947).
Horeb (1838) and Bronllwyn chapels of upper Pentyrch (Cadw 22821; Coflein 9697, 9695).

areas.name: Morganstown and Gelynis
areas.reason: Small Taff-side village of Bethel Chapel (1842) and 19th-century cottages, with Gelynis, a 16th-century gentry farmhouse, and the Morganstown motte.

reasons: 16th-century Gelynis, listed II*, and the motte record a pre-industrial manor site (Cadw 13912; Coflein 95169).
Chapel village that grew with the Taff valley industries (Cadw 13862; Coflein 18304).
Short terraces and a chapel at the foot of the Garth (Coflein 18304; OS one-inch 1947).
Bethel chapel of 1842, the community centre (Cadw 13862).

areas.name: Creigiau and Castell-y-Mynach
areas.reason: Station hamlet of Creigiau with its smithy-post office and church hall, and the late-medieval mansion of Castell-y-Mynach in its own grounds.

reasons: Late-medieval hall-house, remodelled in the 17th century, with 16th-17th-century outbuildings (Coflein 300587, 37489).
Gentry seat and farming hamlet that became a railway village (Coflein 300587).
Thatched post office, farm and mansion among fields (Coflein 409475, 18444).
Post office and 1913 church hall served the hamlet (Coflein 409475; Cadw 22828).

areas.name: Old Radyr (St John's church and Radyr Court)
areas.reason: Medieval parish church of Radyr with its walled churchyard, and Radyr Court, a 16th-century house on a medieval settlement site.

reasons: Medieval church and deserted medieval settlement sites (Cadw 13780; Coflein 15444, 15443).
Original parish centre before the railway village grew (Coflein 19341).
Church and manor house in fields above the Taff (OS one-inch 1947; Coflein 19341).
Parish church and walled churchyard (Cadw 13780, 13781).

areas.name: Gwent Levels (Wentloog Level, Cardiff section)
areas.reason: An outstanding reclaimed coastal wetland landscape whose sea walls, reens, field pattern, wharves and scattered farms record continuous drainage and enclosure from the Roman period onwards; in 1947 the same reen-drained levels ran unbroken west to the River Rhymney.

reasons: Roman drainage ditches, 1591 sea wall, reen grid and 16th-18th-century farms (Coflein 519317, 275880, 19334).
Continuous reclamation and enclosure of the Wentloog Level since the Roman period (Coflein 519317; Cadw GM474).
Rectilinear reen-drained levels, sea walls and scattered farms (OS one-inch 1947).
Farming communities and wharves of the Levels (Coflein 506654, 506709).

areas.name: Cardiff Docks and Butetown
areas.reason: The complete working landscape of what Coflein calls, at the time, 'the biggest coal port in the world': five Bute docks with their locks, basins, coal hoists and staithes, the sea pound of the Glamorganshire Canal and the Taff Vale Railway terminus, with the planned Butetown grid, its exchange and shipping offices and the Pierhead; the seaward terminus of the coal and iron landscapes already registered upstream.

reasons: Dock walls, locks, basins and graving docks of 1798-1907; buried masonry in filled docks (Coflein 34288, 400534).
Bute docks exporting valley coal; per Coflein, the world's biggest coal port (Coflein 91412).
Geometric docks, rail fans and hoists against the Butetown grid and Pierhead (Cadw 14055; OS six-inch 1947).
Wales' oldest multi-ethnic community: seamen's missions, Norwegian Church, mosques (Coflein 420177, 302127, 9321, 11800).

areas.name: Taff Gorge: Melingriffith and Pentyrch iron and tinplate landscape
areas.reason: A compact early industrial landscape in the Taff Gap where the Melingriffith tinplate works, Pentyrch furnaces and forge, the Little Garth haematite mines, the Melingriffith weir, feeder and pump, the Glamorganshire Canal and the Melingriffith and Pentyrch tramroad were linked, overlooked by Castell Coch; it falls short because the ironworks had closed and the ensemble was already fragmentary and small beside registered landscapes.

reasons: Weir, feeder, pump, tramroad and works sites; furnaces and forge since cleared (Coflein 34440, 91548, 34112).
Linked Pentyrch iron and Melingriffith tinplate system from c.1749 (Coflein 40456, 34111, 91548).
Wooded Taff gorge overlooked by Castell Coch (OS one-inch 1947; Cadw GM206).
Works communities of Gwaelod-y-Garth and Melingriffith (Gwaelod-y-Garth appraisal p.6; Melingriffith appraisal pp.6-7).

areas.name: Craig y Parc
areas.reason: Well-preserved Arts and Crafts garden by C.E. Mallows, integrated with his house and lodge, laid out 1913-15.

reasons: Garden as built 1913-15; kitchen garden not yet taken by school buildings in 1947 (Cadw PGW(Gm)6).
Designed by C.E. Mallows for coal owner Thomas 'small coal' Evans (Cadw PGW(Gm)6).
Per Cadw, well-preserved axial Arts and Crafts terraced garden integrated with the house (Cadw PGW(Gm)6).
Private house garden in 1947; no evidence of wider meaning.

areas.name: Cathays Cemetery
areas.reason: Large Victorian multi-denominational cemetery of 1859 by R.G. Thomas and T. Waring, retaining its heart-shaped layout, chapels, lodge and evergreen planting.

reasons: Original 1859 heart-shaped layout; RC chapel possibly standing in 1947 (Cadw PGW(Gm)19; Coflein 11777).
Cardiff New Cemetery, multi-denominational, by R.G. Thomas and T. Waring (Cadw PGW(Gm)19).
Gothic gateway, twin chapels and conifer-lined axial walks (Cadw PGW(Gm)19).
The town's principal burial ground since 1859, with sections and chapels for each faith (Cadw PGW(Gm)19).

areas.name: Parc Cefn Onn (The Dingle)
areas.reason: Early twentieth-century woodland garden laid out by E.A. Prosser and his head gardener Tom Jenkins, with exotic conifers, rhododendrons and azaleas.

reasons: Woodland garden of c.1911-33; only the northern Dingle planted by 1947 (Cadw PGW(Gm)20).
Made by E.A. Prosser of the Taff Vale Railway and gardener Tom Jenkins (Cadw PGW(Gm)20).
Rustic paths, rills, cascades and fine conifers, rhododendrons and azaleas (Cadw PGW(Gm)20).
Council park from 1944; summerhouse built for Prosser's sick son (Cadw PGW(Gm)20).

areas.name: Sophia Gardens
areas.reason: The first public park in Cardiff and the earliest in Wales, opened 1858 and designed by Alexander Roos for the Bute estate, with axial avenue, circle, fountain and bandstand.

reasons: 1858-1901 layout, now overlain by sports buildings, largely intact in 1947 (Cadw PGW(Gm)21).
First public park in Wales, by Bute architect Alexander Roos, opened 1858 (Cadw PGW(Gm)21).
Axial double avenue, railed circle, fountain and bandstand; lodge bombed in WWII (Cadw PGW(Gm)21).
Opened to compensate townspeople for the closing of the castle grounds (Cadw PGW(Gm)21).

areas.name: Cardiff Castle and Bute Park
areas.reason: Castle grounds landscaped by Capability Brown (1778) and the 3rd Marquess's park laid out by Andrew Pettigrew from 1871, one of the largest urban landscapes in Wales.

reasons: Brown's 1778 walks and Pettigrew's 1870s layout and planting survive (Cadw PGW(Gm)22).
Capability Brown, Andrew Pettigrew and the Bute family; passed to the city in 1947 (Cadw PGW(Gm)22).
Per Cadw, one of the largest urban parks; open flowing design setting the castle (Cadw PGW(Gm)22).
Given to the city on the 4th Marquess's death in 1947 and opened to the public (Cadw PGW(Gm)22).

areas.name: Victoria Park, Cardiff
areas.reason: Small Victorian public park of 1894-97 retaining its layout, with bandstand site and the listed Macfarlane fountain canopy of 1908.

reasons: 1894-97 layout intact in 1947, with the ornamental lake and two fountains (Cadw PGW(Gm)23).
Diamond Jubilee park on Ely Common, with zoo and Billy the seal 1912-39 (Cadw PGW(Gm)23).
Winding paths, lake, bandstand and 1908 Macfarlane fountain canopy (Cadw PGW(Gm)23).
Popular local park; animals given by returning sea captains; Samuel family memorial (Cadw PGW(Gm)23).

areas.name: Roath Park
areas.reason: Ambitious late Victorian public park by William Harpur and W.W. Pettigrew (1887-94), with the 29-acre lake, botanic garden, wild garden and recreation ground.

reasons: Original framework, dam, bridges and educational Students' Garden in place in 1947 (Cadw PGW(Gm)24).
Cardiff's first publicly owned park, by Harpur and Pettigrew on Bute land (Cadw PGW(Gm)24).
Per Cadw, fine late Victorian park; the 29-acre lake an outstanding feature (Cadw PGW(Gm)24).
Boating, bathing and recreation since 1894; Scott Memorial to the Antarctic party (Cadw PGW(Gm)24).

areas.name: Cathays Park (Alexandra, Gorsedd and Friary Gardens)
areas.reason: Edwardian civic gardens by William Harpur (1903-06), set within the Cathays Park civic centre and centred on the Welsh National War Memorial.

reasons: Edwardian layouts of 1903-06 retained (Cadw PGW(Gm)26).
Gardens of the 1897 Bute sale; Gorsedd circle from the 1899 Eisteddfod (Cadw PGW(Gm)26).
Formal gardens set in the civic centre with the War Memorial as focal point (Cadw PGW(Gm)26).
Welsh National War Memorial, Gorsedd circle and statues of national figures (Cadw PGW(Gm)26).

areas.name: Insole Court
areas.reason: Grand Victorian and Edwardian town garden of the Insole family, with terraces, Pulhamite rockwork and Violet Insole's nationally known iris and alpine collections.

reasons: Terraces, Pulhamite rockwork and 1880s planting survive (Cadw PGW(Gm)27).
Insole coal family; Violet Insole's nationally recognised iris and alpine collections (Cadw PGW(Gm)27).
Balustraded terraces and rockwork water garden (Cadw PGW(Gm)27).
Corporation-owned from 1932; Cardiff ARP headquarters in WWII (Cadw LB 14127).

areas.name: Rookwood
areas.reason: Informal Victorian grounds of Rookwood laid out by Col. Sir Edward Stock Hill (1866-1902), with fine specimen trees, a Gothic summerhouse mound and lodges.

reasons: Victorian grounds on a 1776 summerhouse site; north field still open in 1947 (Cadw PGW(Gm)28).
Col. Sir Edward Stock Hill's grounds, 1866-1902; hospital from 1917 (Cadw PGW(Gm)28).
Informal lawns with cedar and wellingtonia, Gothic summerhouse on its mound (Cadw PGW(Gm)28).
Hospital grounds from 1917; trees planted for Hill family births (Cadw PGW(Gm)28).

areas.name: Waterloo Gardens, Roath Mill Gardens and Roath Brook Gardens
areas.reason: Group of Edwardian public gardens along the Roath Brook, given by Lord Tredegar and designed by W.W. Pettigrew.

reasons: Path layouts little changed from the 1919-20 OS maps (Cadw PGW(Gm)29).
Edwardian gardens on Lord Tredegar's gift, designed by W.W. Pettigrew (Cadw PGW(Gm)29).
Lawns, informal trees and caretaker's shelter along the Roath Brook (Cadw PGW(Gm)29).
Opened with civic ceremonies 1910 and 1912; paddling pool and rockery (Cadw PGW(Gm)29).

areas.name: St Fagans Castle
areas.reason: Multi-period terraced and compartmented garden with medieval fishponds, Pulham water garden and the Earl of Plymouth's 1908 woodland of axial rides.

reasons: Medieval fishponds, Tudor structure and the complete 1908 woodland rides in 1947 (Cadw PGW(Gm)31).
Plymouth estate seat; castle given for the national folk museum in 1947 (St Fagans appraisal pp.4-5).
Per Cadw, one of the most important historic gardens in Wales (Cadw PGW(Gm)31).
Private estate garden in 1947; museum use followed the gift (St Fagans appraisal pp.4-5).

areas.name: Pontcanna Fields and Llandaff Fields
areas.reason: Late Victorian extension of the Taff-side parkland (1879; Llandaff Fields 1898-1901) with the great axial lime avenue, forming one green tract with Sophia Gardens and Bute Park.

reasons: 1898-1901 layout with great axial avenue; 1920s baths and features partly surviving (Cadw PGW(Gm)59).
Llandaff Fields saved from building by a newspaper campaign, 1898 (Cadw PGW(Gm)59).
Per Cadw, magnificent axial lime avenue, a very striking feature (Cadw PGW(Gm)59).
Cricket, hockey, tennis and open-air baths for the city (Cadw PGW(Gm)59).

areas.name: Whitchurch Hospital
areas.reason: Core of the therapeutic landscaped grounds of the Edwardian Cardiff City Mental Hospital (1902-08), with Pettigrew planting, octagonal shelters and the Velindre grounds.

reasons: Asylum grounds of 1902-08 with six octagonal shelters (Cadw PGW(Gm)66).
Per Cadw, one of the most important Edwardian asylums in Wales; military hospital in both wars (Cadw PGW(Gm)66).
Formal axis to the chapel, informal ward gardens and fine trees (Cadw PGW(Gm)66).
Therapeutic grounds for patients, linked to the nursing regime (Cadw PGW(Gm)66).

areas.name: Coryton House
areas.reason: Formal terraces and informal water garden of the Cory family's town house, laid out c.1900 and enlarged 1915-40.

reasons: Layout complete by the 1940 OS map, with lodge, orchard and kitchen garden (Cadw PGW(Gm)67).
Town house of James Herbert Cory of the shipowning Cory family (Cadw PGW(Gm)67).
Balustraded terraces with Irish yews and pavilions, informal water garden (Cadw PGW(Gm)67).
Private house garden; no evidence of wider meaning.

areas.name: Thompson's Park (Sir David's Field)
areas.reason: Victorian park opened in 1891 by Charles Thompson of Spillers and enlarged c.1895 by William Goldring, with lake, Dell, fountain pool and Goscombe John's 'Joyance'.

reasons: Layout and fan-shaped bed on the 1947 OS; original 'Joyance' statue in place (Cadw PGW(Gm)71).
Opened 1891 by Charles Thompson of Spillers; enlarged by William Goldring (Cadw PGW(Gm)71).
Lake, Dell, fountain pool and Goscombe John's 'Joyance' (Cadw PGW(Gm)71).
Private park opened to the people of Cardiff in 1891; Edwardian bowling green (Cadw PGW(Gm)71; Coflein 413406).

areas.name: Grange Gardens
areas.reason: Small Victorian park of 1891-95 on land given by Lords Bute and Windsor, with central bandstand and radial paths to five entrances.

reasons: 1890s radial layout as on the six-inch 1947; fountain canopy gone in 1943 (Cadw PGW(Gm)72).
Land given by Lords Bute and Windsor; Cardiff's first park with a bandstand (Cadw PGW(Gm)72).
Radial paths from the central bandstand to five entrances (Cadw PGW(Gm)72).
Grangetown's park, with its 1920s war memorial (Cadw PGW(Gm)72).

areas.name: Ty Gwyn
areas.reason: Eclectic Edwardian garden of the builder James E. Turner (house 1906, terraces dated 1926), with Japanese water garden, pavilions and walled kitchen garden.

reasons: Little altered; glasshouses and paddock still part of the garden in 1946 (Cadw PGW(Gm)76).
Garden of James E. Turner, builder of the Cathays Park civic centre (Cadw PGW(Gm)76).
Per Cadw, eclectic grand garden with authentic Japanese garden and fine pavilions (Cadw PGW(Gm)76).
Private house garden; no evidence of wider meaning.

areas.name: Loudoun Square garden, Butetown
areas.reason: Enclosed central garden of the Bute estate's principal residential square in Butetown, the social heart of the docks community, cleared in the post-war redevelopment.

reasons: Map only: central enclosure, perimeter path and small structure; 1880 presence unchecked (OS six-inch 1947).
Planned centre of the Bute estate's Butetown suburb (Coflein 33120; MSS appraisal p.30).
Map only: plain lawn with a perimeter walk (OS six-inch 1947).
Square framed by Bethania (1854) and Wesleyan (1856) chapels, heart of Tiger Bay (Coflein 9322, 9384, 33120).

areas.name: Adamsdown (Old) Cemetery
areas.reason: Early Victorian municipal cemetery of Cardiff, closed in 1877, with a mortuary chapel and memorials to seamen of the Bute Docks.

reasons: Municipal cemetery closed 1877; mortuary chapel on the 1889 25-inch (Coflein 402727, 402726).
Early public cemetery of Cardiff; many memorials to Bute Docks seamen (Coflein 402727).
Map only: small, plainly laid-out walled ground (OS six-inch 1947).
Burial ground of the docks community, with seamen's gravestones (Coflein 402727).

areas.name: Splott Park
areas.reason: Edwardian public park of 18 acres given by Lord Tredegar in 1901, with bandstand (1904), sports grounds, bowling green (1906) and open-air baths (1922).

reasons: Edwardian features dated 1901-22; 1922 baths replaced in 1976 (Coflein 411742, 415046).
Lord Tredegar's gift of 1901 to the Corporation (Coflein 411742).
Mainly a recreation ground with few ornamental features (Coflein 411742; OS one-inch 1947).
Bandstand, pitches, bowling green, quoits, tennis and open-air baths for Splott (Coflein 411742, 415046).

areas.name: Heath Park (Heath House grounds)
areas.reason: Country-house grounds of Heath House with walled garden, parterres, formal garden, parkland, lodge and carriage drive, later taken for the airfield, playing fields and hospital.

reasons: Walled garden, parterres, lodge and drive recorded on the 1901 25-inch (Coflein 265782).
Heath House grounds used for a US Army camp and landing ground in 1944 (Coflein 414036).
Fuller 1901 features than Rookwood, but already cut by the airfield (Coflein 265782, 414036).
Wartime camp; King George V Field laid out only after the war (Coflein 411696).

areas.name: Llandaff Court (Bishop's Palace) grounds
areas.reason: Eighteenth-century house grounds beside the cathedral green, with gatehouse, lodges, lawns, parterres and walks, for whose privacy the old road was diverted.

reasons: Gatehouse, lodges, lawns, parterres and walk on the 1901 25-inch (Coflein 265792).
18th-century setting of Llandaff Court; the road was diverted for its privacy (Llandaff appraisal p.29).
Lawns and parterres by the cathedral green; design undocumented (Coflein 265792).
Private house grounds; no evidence of wider meaning in 1947 (Coflein 265792).

areas.name: Llandaff Cathedral Bell Tower
areas.reason: Ruined 13th-century detached bell tower of Llandaff Cathedral; of national importance for the organisation and practice of medieval Christianity.

reasons: Per Cadw, 13th-century tower walls to 4.5 m with chronology and building-technique potential (Cadw GM013).
Detached bell tower of Llandaff Cathedral; illustrates medieval Christian practice (Cadw GM013).
Degraded rubble ruin with gaps; group value with palace and cathedral (Cadw GM013; Coflein 32796).
Ruin in the cathedral precinct; no evidence of its own use or meaning (Cadw GM013).

areas.name: Leckwith Bridge
areas.reason: Medieval three-arched rubble bridge over the Ely, recorded by Leland in 1536; of national importance for medieval construction and transport.

reasons: Per Cadw, medieval pointed double-ringed arches with 17th- and 18th-century rebuilds; structural potential (Cadw GM014).
Ely crossing Leland called 'soundly built of stone' in 1536; bypassed 1934 (Cadw GM014).
Three-arched rubble bridge with refuges over cutwaters and slab-topped parapets (Cadw GM014).
Disused crossing by 1947; no evidence of local meaning (Cadw GM014).

areas.name: Twmpath, Rhiwbina
areas.reason: Well-preserved ditched medieval motte; of national importance for medieval defensive practices.

reasons: Per Cadw, well-preserved 6 m motte and ditch with structural and deposit potential (Cadw GM017).
Early castle of the medieval Taff-Rhymney uplands; already scheduled in 1930 (Cadw GM017).
Steep grassed mound standing in open fields in 1947 (Cadw GM017; Coflein 307123).
Field monument; no evidence of use or meaning (Coflein 307123).

areas.name: Caerau Camp
areas.reason: Multivallate Iron Age hillfort enclosing a Neolithic causewayed enclosure, a medieval ringwork and churchyard; of national importance for late prehistoric defensive organisation.

reasons: Per Cadw, Neolithic causewayed enclosure, triple-ramparted hillfort, ringwork and church on one hill (Cadw GM018).
Multi-period hilltop from Neolithic to medieval parish centre overlooking Cardiff (Cadw GM018; Coflein 94517).
Triple ramparts enclosing 8.8 ha on a commanding ridge-end above Cardiff (Cadw GM018).
Parish church and churchyard inside the ramparts; 1947 congregation not recorded (Cadw GM018).

areas.name: Cae-yr-Arfau Burial Chamber
areas.reason: Neolithic chambered tomb of three large slabs; of national importance for prehistoric burial and ritual.

reasons: Per Cadw, chamber with likely intact deposits and buried land surface; free-standing in 1947 (Cadw GM030; Coflein 93016).
Neolithic chambered tomb, one of very few in Cardiff (Cadw GM030).
Three-slab chamber with 2 m capstone on a spur above the Ely valley (Cadw GM030).
Funerary monument; no evidence of later local meaning (Coflein 93016).

areas.name: Castle Field Camp E of Craig-Llwyn
areas.reason: Sub-rectangular Iron Age hillfort on a spur of the Cefn Mably ridge; of national importance for later prehistoric defence and settlement.

reasons: Per Cadw, well-preserved banks and berms with chronology and functional potential (Cadw GM066).
Later prehistoric fort on a spur of the Cefn Mably ridge (Cadw GM066; Coflein 301309).
Sub-rectangular banks to 2 m on a knoll with wide views; cut by lime workings (Cadw GM066).
Farmland earthwork; no evidence of use or meaning.

areas.name: Old Bishop's Palace, Llandaff
areas.reason: Late 13th-century fortified palace of the bishops of Llandaff with gatehouse, curtain wall and towers; of national importance for the organisation of medieval Christianity.

reasons: Gatehouse to first floor, curtain to full height, towers and hall fragments (Cadw GM073).
Bishops' seat probably built by William de Braose (1266-87), damaged in the 1404 Glyndwr rising (Cadw GM073).
Castle-like ruined palace above the Taff; group with cathedral and bell tower (Cadw GM073).
Ruins in Llandaff's historic core; 1947 use not recorded in the sources (Cadw GM073).

areas.name: Wenallt Camp, Rhiwbina
areas.reason: Oval univallate Iron Age defended enclosure on a spur above Cardiff; of national importance for later prehistoric settlement.

reasons: Per Cadw, well-preserved stone-revetted bank with considerable archaeological potential (Cadw GM097).
Iron Age enclosure on a spur overlooking Cardiff; Glamorgan Inventory I.2 (Coflein 307793).
Oval bank up to 2.2 m high on a south-facing slope (Cadw GM097).
Crossed by a public footpath; no evidence of meaning (Cadw GM097).

areas.name: Five Round Barrows on Garth Hill
areas.reason: Linear group of five Bronze Age round barrows on the summit of Garth Hill; of national importance for prehistoric burial, with group value.

reasons: Per Cadw, intact burial deposits and buried land surfaces likely; group value (Cadw GM107).
Bronze Age barrow cemetery recording prehistoric funerary ritual (Cadw GM107; Coflein 93060-93062).
Row of five mounds up to 37 m across on the Garth Hill skyline (Cadw GM107).
Hilltop landmark; no evidence of use or meaning in the sources.

areas.name: Cross in Llandaff Cathedral
areas.reason: Late 10th- or early 11th-century moulded pillar cross; of national importance as a relic of early medieval Christianity and sculpture.

reasons: Per Cadw, well-preserved 10th/11th-century Sutton Stone pillar cross with interlace (Cadw GM115).
Early medieval Christian sculpture, stylistically linked to the Llandough cross (Cadw GM115).
Ringed narrow head, exaggerated corner mouldings and plaitwork, 0.89 m high (Cadw GM115).
Christian monument; its 1947 position, well or cathedral, is uncertain (Cadw GM115).

areas.name: Cardiff Castle and Roman Fort

areas.name: Dominican Friary (Blackfriars)

areas.name: Llwynda-Ddu Camp

areas.name: Ely Roman Villa

areas.reason: Water-wheel pump of 1807 by Rennie and Jessop lifting tail-race water from Melingriffith tinplate works into the Glamorganshire Canal; of national importance for early industrial water management.
